covered: Purchase cost and freight, raw materials/work in progress/finished goods, cost assignment, sold versus unsold stock, write-downs and cash timing.
deferred: Detailed production overhead allocation, abnormal waste, taxes, borrowing costs, consignment, biological assets and full IAS 2 measurement/reversal requirements are deferred.

hoverDefinition: Inventory holds the cost of goods awaiting sale or production. Selling stock transfers its carrying cost to expense; paying suppliers and writing stock down are different events.

objectives.statement: Roll purchase costs into inventory and move the cost sold into expense.
objectives.evidence: Reconcile opening stock, purchases, cost sold and closing stock.

objectives.statement: Separate a non-cash inventory write-down from a purchase payment.
objectives.evidence: Calculate inventory and profit after a stated recoverability limit without inventing cash.

context.timeframe: A separate illustrative teaching month. Worked and practice scenarios start independently; they are not consecutive company-case rounds.
assumptions: All inventory is owned and goods transfers qualify for the stated sale recognition.
Freight in the worked example brings goods to saleable location and condition; its stated amount is included in inventory cost.
No tax, discounts, returns, losses or costs other than those stated. Stated cost sold is already assigned consistently.
A stated net realisable value is a teaching measurement assumption; no unmentioned valuation change or financing exists.

framework.limitations: Simplified conceptual teaching scenarios in INR lakh; currency does not establish jurisdiction. Recognition, operating perimeter and cash classifications are stated assumptions. Primary public IFRS overviews provide background, not a claim of compliance. Jurisdiction, reporting period, effective amendments and complete disclosure requirements require separate study.

mechanism.title: Build the cost pool before measuring profit
paragraphs: Inventory is a resource held for sale, being made for sale, or consumed in production. A purchase exchanges cash or creates a supplier obligation for that resource. It does not automatically create a current expense. Include only costs that qualify for the chosen accounting basis; the examples explicitly identify the costs included.

Raw materials enter production, work in progress is unfinished production, and finished goods await sale. A retailer may hold purchased merchandise instead. Movement between these categories changes composition, without by itself creating sales or cash.

mechanism.title: Transfer the cost sold into expense
paragraphs: Opening inventory + qualifying additions − cost sold − losses or write-downs = closing carrying inventory, when no other movements exist. The sales price determines revenue; the assigned carrying cost determines the inventory expense. They are different amounts.

For distinct items, actual identification can be appropriate. FIFO assigns older costs first; weighted average pools comparable costs. A cost formula is an accounting allocation, not necessarily a description of physical dispatch. The worked example supplies the assigned cost sold so no costing convention is hidden.

mechanism.title: Test unsold stock without inventing a receipt
paragraphs: Under the stated lower-of-cost-and-net-realisable-value teaching rule, compare unsold cost with the estimated selling price less completion and selling costs. A shortfall reduces the asset and profit now; it does not collect money. A later sale has its own revenue, carrying-cost release and collection.

The public IAS 2 overview supports this background. It is not a complete cost-allocation or reversal manual. The examples state the recoverable amount directly and defer reversals and specialist inventory rules.

mechanism.title: Keep the stock roll-forward separate from the bank
paragraphs: Credit inventory purchases raise inventory and payables without an immediate cash outflow. Paying a supplier reduces cash and the payable. A cash sale creates an operating receipt; a credit sale first creates a receivable. Stock can therefore fall without cash increasing.
When reconciling profit to cash, a write-down already reflected in net inventory movement must not also be added back without adjusting that movement. A06 develops both consistent approaches.

distinctions.name: Inventory and equipment
distinctions.explanation: Inventory is intended for sale or production consumption; equipment supports operations over time.
distinctions.whenItMatters: The same physical item can have a different role depending on the business.

distinctions.name: Cost and selling price
distinctions.explanation: Cost is the assigned resource amount; selling price is the customer consideration.
distinctions.whenItMatters: Use cost, not revenue, in the inventory roll-forward.

distinctions.name: Cost formula and physical flow
distinctions.explanation: FIFO and weighted average allocate cost; they need not reproduce physical movement.
distinctions.whenItMatters: A change in input prices can change reported margins and closing stock.

distinctions.name: Write-down and sale
distinctions.explanation: A write-down recognises lost recoverability without a customer transaction.
distinctions.whenItMatters: A lower stock balance is not evidence of cash released.

workedExample.setup: Opening cash 40 and inventory 10 are funded by equity 50, with no liabilities. Buy goods for 20 on supplier credit and pay qualifying freight 2 in cash. Sell goods with assigned cost 18 for recognised revenue 30 on credit, collecting 24. Unsold cost is 14; its stated net realisable value is 11. Apply the stated lower-of-cost-and-NRV rule. No supplier principal is paid and no other event occurs.
steps: Inventory cost available = 10 + 20 + 2 = 32. Credit purchases also create a payable of 20; freight uses cash 2.
Expense the assigned cost sold 18. Before the valuation test, unsold cost = 32 − 18 = 14.
Write-down = 14 − 11 = 3. Closing inventory is 11; total inventory expense is 18 + 3 = 21.
Operating cash = customer receipts 24 − freight paid 2 = +22; cash closes at 62. Neither the credit purchase nor the write-down is a cash payment.
Closing assets = cash 62 + receivables 6 + inventory 11 = 79. Payables 20 + equity (50 + 9) 59 = 79.
Using net inventory movement: profit 9 − receivable increase 6 − inventory increase 1 + payable increase 20 = operating cash 22. Do not add the write-down again.
workedExample.result: Inventory closes at 11, profit is 9 and operating cash is +22.
workedExample.interpretation: The goods cost 32 before sale and valuation. The unsold resource is 11, while supplier credit, customer collection and freight determine this month’s cash.

statementEffects.explanation: Complete simplified statement effects for this isolated worked scenario under the stated assumptions.
changes: Income statement: revenue 30, cost sold 18 and write-down 3; profit 9.
Balance sheet: cash 62, receivables 6, inventory 11, trade payables 20 and equity 59.
Cash flow: operating receipts 24 and freight payment 2; net operating +22; no investing or financing cash.

misconceptions.claim: Every inventory purchase is immediately an expense.
misconceptions.correction: Retain the unsold qualifying cost as an asset; expense the carrying cost sold or lost.

misconceptions.claim: Inventory leaves at its selling price.
misconceptions.correction: Release its assigned carrying cost, not the customer price.
misconceptions.diagnostic: Which amount was recorded as inventory?

misconceptions.correction: A write-down is a non-cash asset and profit reduction.

practice.setup: Independent scenario: buy goods for 12 cash and pay qualifying freight 3 cash. Sell part for 16 cash; its assigned cost including allocated freight is 9. No opening inventory, write-down, tax or other event exists.
practice.question: What are closing inventory, profit and operating cash movement?

options.feedback: The unsold cost remains an asset, so payment 15 is not all current expense.
Cost available 15 less cost sold 9 leaves 6. Profit is 16 − 9; cash is 16 − 15.
Releasing revenue 16 instead of cost 9 confuses price with inventory cost.

practice.solution: Inventory = 12 + 3 − 9 = 6. Profit = 16 − 9 = 7. Operating cash = 16 − 12 − 3 = +1. Profit 7 − inventory increase 6 = cash 1.

hints.text: First allocate resource cost between sold and unsold goods, then compute bank movements.
Inventory = 12 + 3 − 9 = 6. Profit = 16 − 9 = 7. Operating cash = 16 − 12 − 3 = +1. Profit 7 − inventory increase 6 = cash 1.

reflection.prompt: Why does profit exceed the cash movement?
rubric: Reconcile profit 7 less inventory increase 6 to cash 1.

practice.setup: Independent scenario: opening inventory is 18. Buy more for 10 cash, sell goods of assigned cost 12 for 20 cash, then value the remaining stock at a stated net realisable value of 13 under the lower-of-cost-and-NRV assumption. No other events, tax or supplier credit exist.
practice.question: Which closing inventory, profit and operating cash movement are consistent?

options.feedback: The write-down 3 does not generate a bank receipt.
Unsold cost 16 exceeds the stated recoverable limit 13.
Unsold cost 16 is written down by 3; only receipts 20 less purchases 10 affect cash.

practice.solution: Unsold cost = 18 + 10 − 12 = 16; write-down = 3; closing inventory = 13. Profit = 20 − 12 − 3 = 5. Operating cash = 20 − 10 = +10. Net inventory falls by 5, so profit 5 − (−5) = cash 10.

hints.text: Separate valuation from receipts and supplier payments.
Unsold cost = 18 + 10 − 12 = 16; write-down = 3; closing inventory = 13. Profit = 20 − 12 − 3 = 5. Operating cash = 20 − 10 = +10. Net inventory falls by 5, so profit 5 − (−5) = cash 10.

reflection.prompt: How can stock fall by 5 while the write-down itself creates no cash?
rubric: Calculate cash from the two bank movements.
Do not add the write-down twice in a net-inventory bridge.
